Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
Jon wrote:
>>This collusion thing seems to be a fairly recent thing...when i first
started playing jyhad 4 years ago it was very rare indeed...Most
players seemed to have only one objective - to roll the table!>>

Deal making is not collusion. Collusion is a secret deal between two or more
players that exists to provide an unfair advantage to one of those players. Two
players making a deal in the middle of a game to split the table is making a
deal, and fully supported by the rules.

Please, everyone, please, use the word collusion correctly. It refers to
something very specific in the VEKN tournament rules.

Messages.Author: LSJ
Messages.Body:
Peter D Bakija wrote:
> players making a deal in the middle of a game to split the table is making a
> deal, and fully supported by the rules.

"Fully supported" only inasfar as the deal doesn't hinder either player's
ability to get the most VPs, yes.

Making a deal to get 2 VPs (and give someone else 3) isn't allowed if you
could get 3 VPs otherwise, for instance.

Making a deal that reduces your ability to gain VPs is not allowed, as the
only reasons for doing so are unsportmanlike or based on out-of-game
considerations.

--
LSJ (vte...@white-wolf.com) V:TES Net.Rep for White Wolf, Inc.

Messages.Author: Johan Lundstrom
Messages.Body:
LSJ <vte...@white-wolf.com> wrote:

>Then the only way you could legally make the deal is if you plan to
>break it. Your partner in the deal will know that. Now, who would
>be your partner in such situations?

Will the other players necessarily know that? Consider this:

Situation:
It's early in the game, say round three or something. I offer my prey
a 3-2 table split (I get the 2). "Sure", he replies. "Judge!" the
others say (and rightly so - my position doesn't really look like it
would be impossible for me to win).

The judge arrives. "Look, I'd like to talk about this in privacy, OK?"
I tell the judge. "I don't want to give a way my deck."
"OK", replies the judge.

Once we're out of hearing range from the other players, I tell the
judge "I don't intend to go through with the deal - I just want my
prey to leave me alone for a while."
"Well, alright then," says the judge.

Question 1: What should the judge tell the other players? Just that
the deal is OK (in which case the other players might think I managed
to convince the judge my situation really *does* suck that badly)? Or
should he elaborate (destroying my plan in the process, and likely
setting the table against me)?

Now, if it's the first case, let's go on:
A good way into the game, it's clear things aren't going as they
should (from my point of view). My prey is in top condition, and is
strong enough to sweep the table no matter what I do. So I decide to
stick to the deal, and it works out. At least I get my two VPs. Phew!

The judge comes by at the end of the game. He doesn't look happy. "I
thought you said you were going to break the deal", he says. "Well," I
respond, "I never got a good situation to do it. Surely I'm not
forbidden to keep a deal just because I intended to break it when I
made it?"

Question 2: Would this be acceptable? If it is, then we have a
problem. Because the deal could be made regardless of the situation
(as I say I'm going to break it), but nothing forces me to break the
deal once I've made it. Thus, I could make a table-splitting deal even
when I'm not in a losing postion.

Messages.Author: Andrew S. Davidson
Messages.Body:
Johan's observations are bang on target as usual. This is why the
judge should be paying no attention to the deals that the players do.
Except in the special case of the Succubus Club, the rules do not
recognise the existence of deals. The players can say what they like
and the judge need pay no attention (except for threats and other
improper speech). What matters is what players actually do - what
game actions do they take. If someone rolls over, e.g. by
transferring out, then that is the point at which the judge should
take action. Justifying this by reference to a deal is irrelevant as
ordinary deals are not binding and so the player is under no
obligation to keep them. He does, however, have a duty to play to win
and maximise his score at all points in time. Rolling over is always
unsportsmanlike. It should be outlawed and I believe that it is.

Andrew

I have no particular interest in defending such, as I recognise the
merits and flaws both ways. I do, however, have an interest in making
sure that the current rules-set is understood.

1) If the current rules-set is universally understood, the rules-set can
be applied consistently, can be applied consistently universally and
can be seen to be applied consistently universally.

2) If the current rules-set is universally understood, clear, thorough,
well-founded arguments can be made. I have seen many, many arguments
flounder due to lack of a coherent lead rather than an inherent,
irresolvable flaw in the argument itself - a point which I've
discussed with LSJ in private e-mail at one point (which is sometimes
why I'll take an argument up with him, to draw a point out fully, in
a manner not entirely dis-similar to his own points many years ago).
Insisting, as Andrew was, that the current rules don't state what
they say through V:EKN and LSJ is stupid in the extreme, and unlikely
to solve anything. Conceding "this is what they say, I grant you,
but I think they should say X, Y and Z because of balancing factors
alpha, beta and gamma, along with pieces of evidence one, two and
three" is far better - hence the reason I followed up Andrew rather
than any of the other posts which actually rationally argue the
points.

I kindly request supporting evidence to this statement.

The relevent section of the tournament rules (copied below) say that a
player must seek to gain the most VPs in a game (at least 3 in a 4-5
player game) and may act on _only_ in-game considerations. Collusion
is, by definition, a deal based on out of game considerations and is
adequately addressed by the rules. Making a losing deal that one does
not intend to honor in order to gain at least 3 VPs, however, is
permissible by a strict interpretation of the rules. (That is not to
say that a judge should not privately question a player for his
reasons for making a losing deal.)

"Players must play each game toward the goal stated in the rulebook of
gaining the most victory points in the current game. Players must not
act on concerns outside the current game (attacking certain players on
the basis of their V:EKN ratings or overall tournament standing,
etc.)."

Messages.Author: Noal McDonald
Messages.Body:
LSJ wrote:
> Players must play to win.
> Not playing to win is against the V:EKN rules. [VEKN 5.2]

I agree. No argument there.

My only point is that the rules, as written, do not prohibit one from
taking a losing deal, even if you can possibly get a majority of the
VPs, if (and only if) it is your intention to not honor the deal, either
by letter or by the spirit. An example of each is below:

Assuming that in a 5 player table (players A, B, C, D and E), you,
player A, strike a deal with player D to work together to oust players
B, C & E and you roll over for player D.

If your intention is to not honor the letter of the deal and, instead of
rolling over, you plan to oust an unsuspecting player D, you are
"playing to win," which, as you stated, is not against the rules.

If you inention is not honor the spirit , but rather the letter of the
deal, and you intend to play a Kindred Restructure or Dramatic Upheaval
so that you end up with the majority of the VPs, you are also "playing
to win."

In both instances, accepting a losing deal is not, as you stated
earlier, against the rules in and of itself. I certainly don't dispute
that a judge is well within his rights to question it. My objection is
regarding the seemingly carte blanche restriction on the type of
*in-game* deals.

Scott, do you disagree with the *entirety* of my assertions?
